To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the two mutations that are known to be responsible for adaptation of 1957 H1N1 and 1968H3N2 pandemic influenza strains to human receptors, when inserted into the HA gene of some recent avain H5N1 strains, enable these strains to bind human receptors and reduce binding to avian receptors, and that these mutations are present in many recent H5N1 avian isolates.
two mutations, when inserted into recent avian HAs, confer the ability to bind human receptors and that these H5N1 HAs are susceptible to acquiring human receptor binding.

the two mutations that are known to enable human receptor binding in pandemic H1N1 and H3N2 influenza viruses, when inserted in recent clade 2 H5N1 avian influenza viruses, enable these viruses to acquire human receptor binding and reduce their threshold for acquiring human transmissibility.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of influenza viruses in the human host, and how these viruses acquire the ability to transmit from person to person.
the molecular mechanisms of influenza virus pathogenesis and transmission in the mammalian host.
the evolution of influenza viruses, and the molecular mechanisms underlying the ability of these viruses to adapt and spread in the human population.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the 2.2 H5N1 strains are more susceptible to adaptation to human receptors than are most H5N1 avian strains.
the H5N1 virus is a high-risk pathogen, and that its potential for adaptation to humans is not limited to the clades 1 and 2.1 viruses.
the H5N1 influenza strains of clade 2 are the most dangerous of all influenza viruses currently circulating in the world.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the 2004-2005 H5N1 avian influenza viruses are more susceptible to acquiring human receptor specificity than previous avian influenza viruses, and therefore, should be monitored more closely for potential emergence of a pandemic strain.
the H5N1 virus clade 2 isolates are more likely to adapt to humans and therefore are more dangerous.
the 2004 H5N1 avian viruses are the most likely to adapt to human transmission.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the recent H5N1 strains are more prone to acquire human receptor specificity and that the mutations responsible for this are already present in some strains.
the recent clade 2 H5N1 avian influenza viruses have an increased propensity to acquire human receptor binding specificity.
the recent H5N1 avian influenza viruses have a higher propensity for acquiring human-like receptor specificity than other avian H5 influenza viruses.
